personality_voice.book_baseline: The Prime Minister in the books is a fully realized viewpoint character with a distinct internal voice. He is anxious, proud, politically defensive, and perpetually out of his depth in magical matters. He experiences genuine fear, resentment, irritation, fleeting moments of dry humor, and occasional unexpected empathy (the 'stab of pity' for Fudge). His voice is marked by hesitation, incomplete sentences, blustering defensiveness when confronted, and a recurring compulsion to appear competent and well-informed even when bewildered. He bristles at being made to feel like 'an ignorant schoolboy,' pushes back against Scrimgeour's encroachments on his authority, and internally processes every magical revelation through the lens of his political self-image. His emotional texture—the sardonic thoughts about his political opponent, the superstitious knocking on wood, the remembered shock of his first meeting with Fudge—is rendered in granular detail across dozens of scenes in HBP Chapter 1.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The Prime Minister does not appear as a character in the film corpus provided. He is referenced obliquely three times: Harry tells Vernon that 'Kingsley is protecting the Muggle Prime Minister' (book scene 68, film scene 1), Vernon mentions seeing Kingsley on the news walking alongside the Prime Minister at a hospital (book scene 69), and Kingsley says 'You're more important' when asked about the Prime Minister (book scene 72, film scene 1). In no film scene does the Prime Minister speak, act, react, or appear as a character with any observable personality or voice.
personality_voice.difference: The entire personality and voice of the Prime Minister—his anxiety, pride, defensiveness, dark humor, political self-consciousness, hesitation, blustering, and emotional complexity—is completely absent from the films. He is reduced to a name mentioned in passing by other characters.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: There is no film portrayal to evaluate. The character's personality and voice are not represented at all. This warrants the lowest possible score. A minimal score of 3 rather than 0 is not warranted either; a score of 0–5 applies when the character is unrecognizable, and here the character is not merely unrecognizable but entirely absent as a speaking, acting subject. Score: 3 (within the 0–5 band for 'unrecognizable,' reflecting that the name at least survives as a reference).

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: The Prime Minister serves a specific and irreplaceable narrative function in HBP: he is the structural device through which Rowling exposes the wizarding world's impact on Muggle society from an outsider's perspective. His scenes provide the reader's first comprehensive account of the catastrophes caused by Voldemort's return—the Brockdale Bridge, the murders, the hurricane, the dementors—framed through a Muggle political consciousness. He also functions as a foil to both Fudge (showing Fudge's political failure through a sympathetic outside eye) and Scrimgeour (establishing the new Minister's authoritarian efficiency). He has genuine agency: he pushes back against Fudge, challenges the narrative ('Good grief, so it's your fault those people were killed'), demands accountability, and tries to assert his authority over Scrimgeour regarding Kingsley and the locked door. He is not passive; he argues, paces, snaps, and confronts.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: In the films, the Prime Minister has no agency whatsoever. He appears only as a noun in other characters' dialogue. Kingsley's protective assignment is mentioned, but the Prime Minister himself neither acts nor is acted upon in any scene. The entire expository and structural function of HBP Chapter 1—delivering the Voldemort-caused disasters to the audience through his perspective—is eliminated. There is no scene in the film corpus where the Prime Minister initiates anything, decides anything, confronts anyone, or changes any event.
narrative_role_agency.difference: Total elimination of narrative role and agency. The character's function as viewpoint expositor, foil, and political counterweight is entirely absent. His confrontations with Fudge and Scrimgeour do not exist in the films.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Role and agency are not reduced—they are eliminated. The score must fall in the 0–5 band ('Role or agency are eliminated or made functionally irrelevant'). Score: 2.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: The Prime Minister's motivations are richly layered: he wants to appear competent and unrattled in the face of incomprehensible magical intrusions; he resents being patronized by Fudge; he is politically self-protective (angry that he cannot explain to the public what is really happening); he experiences genuine fear of the magical world while needing to project control; and he has an internal conflict between his democratic instincts (his office, his decisions, his staff) and his complete powerlessness in the face of wizarding authority. His outburst about Scrimgeour planting Kingsley without his consent is a direct expression of this conflict. He also experiences unexpected human empathy for Fudge that conflicts with his political resentment of him.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: No motivations or internal conflicts are portrayed. The character does not appear as a subject in any film scene.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: Complete absence. None of the motivations or internal conflicts are present.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Motivations and internal conflict are not simplified or altered—they are entirely absent. Score: 2 (within the 0–4 band for 'opposite, absent, or incoherent,' reflecting absence rather than incoherence).

character_arc.book_baseline: The Prime Minister has a meaningful arc within HBP Chapter 1 alone: he moves from a man who has tried to suppress and rationalize the existence of magic (hiding the portrait, giving away the gerbil, training himself not to look) to someone who, by the end of the chapter, is being informed that Britain is at war with a dark wizard and that his own Junior Minister has been cursed. Over the broader book series, he progresses from total ignorance and terror at his first meeting with Fudge to a man who is 'wiser now,' can identify dementors, and understands (however reluctantly) the wizarding world's relationship to Muggle society. This is a flat-to-informed arc: not heroic growth, but a gradual, reluctant accumulation of terrible knowledge. His final moment—'But for heaven's sake, you're wizards!'—captures the endpoint of his arc as someone who has internalized the reality of magic but still cannot accept its limitations.
character_arc.film_portrayal: No arc is present. The character does not appear in any scene where an arc could be observed.
character_arc.penalty_logic: Arc is nonexistent in the films. Score: 1 (within the 0–4 band).

key_relationships.book_baseline: The Prime Minister's two key relationships are with Fudge and Scrimgeour. With Fudge: a dynamic of reluctant, fearful tolerance that evolves into something approaching mutual recognition and even pity—the Prime Minister resents Fudge's condescension but feels genuine sympathy when he sees him diminished and sacked. With Scrimgeour: an immediate power struggle, with the Prime Minister attempting to assert democratic authority ('I decide who works for me') and Scrimgeour ruthlessly overriding him. Both relationships reveal essential things about the Prime Minister's character: his pride, his powerlessness, and his humanity. There is also the relationship with Kingsley—indirect and mediated, but functioning as a background symbol of the wizarding world's quiet intrusion into his life.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The relationship with Kingsley is referenced (Kingsley protects him; the Dursleys like Kingsley), but this is observed from outside, with no dynamic between the Prime Minister and Kingsley actually depicted. The relationships with Fudge and Scrimgeour do not exist in the film corpus.
key_relationships.difference: All key relationships are absent as active dynamics. The Kingsley connection survives as a narrative fact mentioned by others but not as a relationship with observable emotional content.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: Key relationships are absent or functionally irrelevant. Score: 1 (within the 0–2 band).

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: The Prime Minister is one of the most nuanced minor characters in the series precisely because he is the only Muggle viewpoint character given extended interiority. His complexity includes: political vanity coexisting with genuine competence; fear coexisting with stubbornness; resentment of magical authority coexisting with reluctant respect; dark humor about his situation; the tragicomic detail of trying to have the portrait removed; the superstitious knocking on wood; the 'persistent habit of wishing to appear well-informed.' He is simultaneously sympathetic and faintly ridiculous, proud and helpless, competent in his world and completely outmatched in another. This layering is the entire point of his inclusion in the series.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: None of this complexity survives. The character is a name. No nuance, no contradiction, no humor, no interiority, no texture of any kind is present in the film corpus.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: Total loss of all complexity and nuance. The character is reduced from a fully realized interiority to a proper noun referenced in other characters' dialogue.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: Complexity is entirely removed. Score: 1 (within the 0–4 band, reflecting near-total elimination).

comparative.key_observations: The Prime Minister is effectively absent from the film adaptations. His entire appearance in the book series—centered on HBP Chapter 1, one of the most distinctive opening chapters in the series—was cut from the films entirely. He survives only as a proper noun mentioned twice in passing: once by Harry explaining Kingsley's assignment, and once by Vernon noting he saw Kingsley on the news near him. No scene depicts him speaking, acting, reacting, or existing as a character with any interiority. Every dimension of his book characterization—his anxious pride, his political self-consciousness, his dark humor, his relationship with Fudge and Scrimgeour, his arc from ignorance to reluctant knowledge, his narrative function as the Muggle-world mirror for Voldemort's return—is entirely absent. This is not a case of compression or simplification; it is complete omission. The total score of 10 reflects the bare minimum acknowledgment that the character's name and peripheral function (being protected by Kingsley) survive in the films, while everything that constituted the character in the books does not.
